frameworks.name: High-Frequency Low-Duration Training Protocol
frameworks.definition: Six short training sessions per day (10 minutes each, spaced 45 minutes apart) distributed across a longer timeframe instead of consolidated volume, paired with high-carbohydrate low-fat nutrition to minimize fat storage during caloric surplus.

claims.text: A 45-minute cadence of short training sessions creates a nervous-system boost every 45 minutes, acting as a productivity hack by providing regular restorative intervals between work blocks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Regularly spaced nervous-system stimulation resets mental fatigue and sustains focus over longer work periods.

claims.text: Converting dietary surplus calories to body fat is more efficient from carbohydrates (lower conversion loss) than from fat (nearly 100% storage efficiency); therefore, under caloric surplus, consuming 100% of excess calories as carbohydrate rather than fat minimizes total fat gain.
claims.speaker: Greg Knuckles
claims.mechanism: Carbohydrate conversion pathway involves higher metabolic cost; fat storage is direct.

numbers.axis: dietary macronutrient conversion efficiency to body fat

bounded_by: depends on total caloric surplus being present

claims.text: The high-frequency high-volume training protocol (6 sessions daily, 7 sets per exercise) drove substantial strength and mass gains but was not sustainable long-term due to overtraining indicators: compromised joint health (knees, elbows), severe sleep disruption, and nervous-system fatigue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Cumulative central nervous system fatigue and joint stress exceed recovery capacity despite optimal nutrition.
bounded_by: Not sustainable beyond 3-4 months even with elite genetics
Requires immediate de-loading (volume reduction) to prevent injury
Speaker reports genetic advantage that most trainees lack

claims.text: After achieving maximum strength gains on the high-frequency protocol, dialing back total volume while preserving the split frequency (reducing from 7 sets to 5 sets per exercise while maintaining 6 daily sessions) allows sustainable strength retention without overtraining collapse.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Reduced cumulative daily stress on CNS and joints while maintaining stimulus frequency and adaptation signal.

claims.text: The same principle of decomposing one large unit into smaller frequent units (successful in training—six 10-minute sessions vs. one 60-minute session) applies identically to business scaling: break large projects into smaller cadenced increments to maintain sustained output and stress recovery.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Frequency of stimulus combined with recovery windows compounds volume tolerance without systemic breakdown.
bounded_by: applies when recovery capacity is the binding constraint, not capital or market size

examples.text: Alex Hormozi trained six times per day for 10 minutes each, with sessions spaced 45 minutes apart. Each session consisted of one set on three exercises. He paired this with a diet of 200 grams protein and 800 grams carbohydrates daily with essentially zero dietary fat. Within this protocol, he gained significant weight and strength across all major lifts (squat, bench, deadlift). However, after several months, he experienced joint pain (knees and elbows), severe sleep disruption from overtraining, and nervous-system fatigue. He then reduced volume to five sets per exercise while maintaining the six-daily-session frequency, which allowed him to retain strength gains without the overtraining collapse.

practices.text: Use a timer and structured 45-minute cadence to schedule frequent short work/training blocks; each block provides a nervous-system reset for sustained cognitive and physical performance.
When consuming a caloric surplus, maximize carbohydrate intake and minimize fat intake to reduce the absolute amount of body fat stored during the surplus phase.
De-load training volume (reduce sets or reps while maintaining session frequency) when joint pain, sleep disruption, or mood degradation signal overtraining.
